title: Comfort ye (Isaiah 40)
hook: speak to the heart of Jerusalem; they that hope in the Lord shall run and not be weary

segments.voice: Yesterday, a shoot, netser, from the stump of Jesse, and the seven gifts of the Spirit. Your line was wisdom, understanding, counsel. Which gift did you ask for? Day four hundred nineteen.

Handel's Messiah begins, after the overture, with a single tenor voice, almost alone, singing two words, and then singing them again: Comfort ye. Handel set the King James wording. But the words were written for people who needed them far more than a concert crowd. Five days ago on this path, Jerusalem burned and its people were marched to Babylon. Isaiah chapter forty sounds like a voice reaching those exiles, after years of silence by foreign rivers. And the very first thing God says is not a scolding.
screen: `A TENOR, ALMOST ALONE.` → `WORDS FOR EXILES.` → `NOT A SCOLDING.`

segments.voice: In the King James: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God." The Douay-Rheims: "Be comforted, be comforted, my people." Said twice, the way you'd say it to a crying child. Then, in the Douay: "Speak ye to the heart of Jerusalem." Some readers hear in that Hebrew phrase a way of saying speak tenderly, the way someone speaks to win back a person they love. Her time of punishment is over. Her sin is forgiven. Then a voice cries out: prepare the way of the Lord in the desert, make a straight road. Every valley lifted up, every mountain made low. Christians know this voice: all four Gospels apply it to John the Baptist, getting the road ready for Jesus. Then a sobering line: all flesh is grass, and the flower fades, but the word of our God stands for ever. And then the image that ends the chapter. God, who never grows tired, gives strength to the weary. Young people stumble and fall. "But they that hope in the Lord shall renew their strength, they shall take wings as eagles, they shall run and not be weary, they shall walk and not faint." Notice the order: soar, run, walk. Not every day is a flying day. Sometimes the promise is simply to keep walking. Some scholars call these later chapters Second Isaiah and set them in the exile; the Church receives the whole book as Isaiah's, read as one. Jewish communities read this chapter on the Sabbath after their fast for the fallen Temple, and call that Sabbath Nachamu, comfort.
screen: `COMFORT YE, COMFORT YE.` · `SPEAK TO THE HEART OF JERUSALEM.` · `PREPARE THE WAY OF THE LORD.` · `SOAR, RUN, WALK.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL RUN AND NOT BE WEARY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: comfort someone today. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's been in a long exile of their own. Grief that hasn't lifted. A diagnosis. Loneliness. A job search that keeps going nowhere. Don't plan a speech. Think about how to speak to their heart: one tender, simple sentence that says, it's not over, and you're not forgotten. Picture saying it, or writing it. If you pray, you can ask God to comfort them, twice, the way Isaiah says it. The bell holds the time.
Comfort ye. God's first words to his exiled people in Isaiah forty, said twice, tenderly: the end of punishment and the start of the road home. Today's word.
Your line: comfort, my people. Today, send your one tender sentence to the person you thought of. Day four hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Isaiah 40 in Advent, including the Second Sunday of Advent in one year of the cycle, and the voice crying in the wilderness is heard as John the Baptist preparing the way for Christ.

original.note: Hebrew: comfort ye, the chapter's first word. It gives its name to Shabbat Nachamu in the Jewish year.

trapdoor: what you thought: the opening of Handel's Messiah.
what it means: God's tender first word to exiles who'd lost everything: comfort, forgiveness, a road home, and strength to keep walking.
what a scholar hears: speak to the heart is a Hebrew idiom for wooing, speaking tenderly; and some scholars date chapters 40–55 to the exile, while the Church reads Isaiah as one book.

notes: Handel composed Messiah in 1741; premiered in Dublin in April 1742. 'Comfort ye' is the first vocal number, for tenor. Confirm.
Second Isaiah (chapters 40–55) is the common scholarly view; the Church's position is described as receiving and reading the book as one. Confirm the Keeper is comfortable with this phrasing.
Shabbat Nachamu follows Tisha b'Av and takes its name from Isaiah 40:1; mentioned as a neighbor practice. Confirm.
Isaiah 40:1–5, 9–11 is the first reading for the Second Sunday of Advent, Year B; confirm.
'Speak to the heart' as an idiom of tender persuasion (cf. Genesis 34:3; Hosea 2:14): confirm.
